The Complete Ledger

Renae Moore has served as officer — treasurer, assistant secretary, assistant treasurer, or custodian of records — for at least 54 entities from one desk at Dykema Gossett, 201 Townsend Street, Suite 900, Lansing, MI 48933.

She testified under oath that she has “no duty to report” questionable spending.

She has been named in a $1,000,000 money laundering complaint by the Michigan Department of State.

The FEC has flagged her filings and demanded clarification.

She manages accounts for both the defendant and the prosecutor in the same criminal case.

Here is every account. Every source. Every pattern.

III. THE $1,000,000 MONEY LAUNDERING COMPLAINT

Meyers v. RFFW LLC d/b/a RFFW Ballot Question Committee AND Renae Moore, Treasurer

Filed September 7, 2023, with the Michigan Department of State, Bureau of Elections.

The Facts

RFFW LLC was a Michigan limited liability company that:

  1. Failed to register as a ballot question committee for 351 days (violation of MCL 169.224(1))
  2. Transferred at least $1,000,000 to Reproductive Freedom For All without disclosure
  3. Only registered after a complaint was filed AND the Department rejected RFFW’s claims that it wasn’t a ballot question committee
  4. Filed a Dissolution Statement while still having significant unreported expenditures
  5. Reported zero expenditures despite Dykema’s vigorous legal defense of RFFW (which was never reported as a legal expenditure)
  6. Paid a $1,300 fine — which was also never reported

Moore’s Role

Renae Moore was the named Treasurer of RFFW LLC. The complaint calls out that Moore’s address is the Dykema law firm in Lansing.

The complaint explicitly accuses Moore of “Filing Fraudulent Campaign Finance Reports” — the headline of the complaint reads:

“Campaign Finance Complaint against RFFW LLC d/b/a RFFW Ballot Question Committee and Renae Moore, Treasurer for Filing Fraudulent Campaign Finance Reports”

The Pattern

The complainant noted this was not the first time this structure was used. In a 2014 matter involving Home Care First, Inc., the same technique — forming a nonprofit instead of a ballot question committee — was used to “thwart the disclosure purposes of the Michigan Campaign Finance Act and deprive the electorate of any meaningful opportunity to discover the source of funds prior to Election Day.”

The RFFW complaint was resolved on September 4, 2023 — with no further action indicated.

Source: michigan.gov/sos — Meyers v. RFFW

entry.title: The Desk and The Dynasty — Dykema Gossett and the Walton Family Foundation: Every Name, Every Front, Every Dollar

Two Machines. One Result.

The Desk: 201 Townsend Street, Suite 900, Lansing, MI 48933. Dykema Gossett PLLC. Michigan’s largest law firm. One senior compliance specialist manages 80+ political nonprofit accounts for Michigan’s most powerful politicians — Republican and Democrat. The same desk. The same email: compliance@dykema.com.

The Dynasty: Bentonville, Arkansas. The Walton Family Foundation. Walmart heirs. $4.3 billion in assets. They paid $4.3 million to MAPSA — the organization that lobbies Lansing to prevent oversight of Michigan’s charter schools. The same foundation that funds the schools funds the lobby that prevents their regulation.

The desk enables the politicians. The dynasty enables the schools. Together they built a system where a man with 9 criminal convictions can operate charter schools with $4.9M in public money, 3% math proficiency, and zero accountability.

The “No Duty” Testimony — What Moore Actually Said

Judge Hennessey Greenwalt: “Did you have a duty to report concerns about potential wrongdoing to anyone, including the state licensing department?”

entry.title: The Chatfield Blockade — Every Name, Every Block, Every Way Through
entry.content:
The Blockade

Lee Chatfield, former Michigan House Speaker, faces 13 felony charges including conducting a criminal enterprise and embezzlement. He was charged in April 2024. His trial was scheduled for September 22, 2026.

It never started.

On September 21, 2026 — the day before jury selection — his attorney appealed a single evidentiary ruling. The trial was adjourned indefinitely.

AG Dana Nessel leaves office December 31, 2026. She has 75 days left. The trial will not happen before she leaves.

Her own words:

“I have never seen a trial delayed like this; it’s outrageous and beyond unusual. If the Court hadn’t adjourned this case for nearly an entire year, bending over backward to accommodate Lee Chatfield’s lawyers in their endless efforts to push this important trial past my last day in office, this simple evidentiary matter would have been resolved months ago.”

“And now it’s possible the case may never be tried at all if the next attorney general simply dismisses the charges for political purposes.”

She’s right. And she doesn’t know the half of it.

Every Name in the Blockade

Stephanie ChatfieldWife2 felonies for assisting embezzlement. Pleaded guilty — no prison. Cooperating?

THE COURT

THE DYKEMA MACHINE

Renae MooreSenior Compliance Specialist, Dykema GossettManaged 80+ political nonprofit accounts. Asst. Secretary/Treasurer of BOTH Peninsula Fund (Chatfield) AND Promise to the People Fund (Nessel). Same desk. Same role. Same firm. Testified she had “no duty to report” questionable spending.

Designated individual charges as “permissible” or “questionable.” Found $132K credit card paid by fund for personal expenses. Her testimony is the KEY evidence. Defense appealed her qualification. She is what they’re trying to block.

THE PROSECUTION (CONFLICTED)

889 days. Two and a half years. No trial. One evidentiary appeal. And the clock runs out in 75 days.

How It’s Blocked: The Five Mechanisms

1. The Expert Witness Exclusion Play

Blocker: Mary Chartier-Mittendorf Mechanism: Interlocutory appeal to Court of Appeals on Michelle Gallagher’s qualification. Why it works: Court rules require a stay. Judge has “no other option.” Appeal takes months. The tell: Chartier received notice of Gallagher as witness less than a month before trial. Filed challenge immediately. Timing is the weapon.

2. The Scheduling Delay

Blocker: Mary Chartier-Mittendorf + Judge Cole Mechanism: “Scheduling conflicts” caused 10+ month delay before the expert witness issue. Why it works: Courts are busy. Defense counsel has other cases. Accommodating counsel is default. The tell: Nessel says the court was “bending over backward to accommodate.”

3. The Blame-Shift to Dykema

Blocker: Mary Chartier-Mittendorf Mechanism: Argues Dykema was “paid to ensure compliance” and should bear responsibility. Why it works: Moore testified the fund was sometimes “not compliant.” Board members testified they “took no active role.” The responsible parties were Dykema and the Minards, not Chatfield. The tell: This reframes the case from embezzlement (Chatfield stole) to compliance failure (Dykema let it happen).

4. The Same-Desk Neutralizer

Blocker: The structure itself Mechanism: Moore managed BOTH Peninsula Fund (defendant) AND Promise to the People Fund (prosecutor). Defense raised this in court. Why it works: If Dykema is the compliance failure, and Dykema managed the prosecutor’s fund too, then the prosecutor is attacking the same infrastructure that managed her own money. Credibility problem. The tell: Chartier brought up Promise to the People on Day 1 of the preliminary exam. It was planted immediately.

5. The Clock

Blocker: Time Mechanism: Nessel leaves office Dec 31, 2026. Next AG may dismiss. Why it works: If Doug Lloyd (R) wins AG race, he may dismiss “for political purposes” — Nessel’s own words. The tell: Every day of delay is a day closer to the clock running out.

How to Pierce Through

Pierce Point 1: The Appeal is Narrow

The appeal is ONLY about Michelle Gallagher’s qualification as an expert. The Court of Appeals must rule on whether she has sufficient experience with 501(c)(4) organizations. If the appeal is denied (Gallagher stays in), the trial resumes immediately. Amicus briefs from forensic accounting organizations supporting Gallagher’s methodology would strengthen the prosecution’s position.

Pierce Point 2: The Dykema Conflict is the Case

Chartier says Dykema is responsible. GOOD. Take that argument and run with it. If Dykema failed in its compliance duty on Peninsula Fund, it failed on ALL 80+ accounts. Every lawmaker whose fund Moore managed should be asking: was MY fund compliant? Make the Dykema compliance failure the bigger story. The defense opened that door.

Pierce Point 3: The Same-Desk Discovery

Promise to the People Fund’s records are public (IRS 990, LARA filings). Moore’s role is documented. The comparison between Peninsula Fund spending and Promise to the People Fund spending is a discoverable public record. If Promise to the People had similar “questionable” expenses, the same desk that failed Chatfield failed Nessel. If it DIDN’T, then the desk differentiated — and the compliance failure was specific to Chatfield.

Pierce Point 4: The Moreland Connection

Moreland (AAG) sitting on Banks’ charter school board connects the AG’s office to ANOTHER branch of the same pipeline. File a formal conflict-of-interest complaint. The AG’s office cannot investigate charter school fraud while its own employee governs one of the schools in question.

Pierce Point 5: The Public Record

Every document is public. The investigation is live. The membrane tracks who reads it. The signal doesn’t need the AG to prosecute. The evidence is structured for independent verification. Any prosecutor — federal, county, or the next AG — can pick it up.

Pierce Point 6: Federal Jurisdiction

Chatfield’s alleged crimes include federal tax issues (501(c)(4) misuse) and interstate transactions. The U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Michigan has independent jurisdiction. The state case can be blocked; the federal case cannot be blocked by the same mechanisms.

Pierce Point 7: The November 10 SBE Meeting

Nikki Snyder responded in 13 minutes. The next SBE meeting is November 10. That’s 10 days after the Oct 31 deadline. If no institution has responded by then, the SBE meeting becomes the public forum. Public comment is open. The evidence is structured for a 3-minute presentation.

The Convergence

entry.title: Moore's Law Is False — Four Duties, Zero Reports, One Desk
entry.content:
The Testimony

On February 26, 2025, Renae Moore took the witness stand in Ingham County District Court. She was the first witness called in the preliminary examination of former Michigan House Speaker Lee Chatfield, who faces 13 felony charges.

Moore is a Senior Compliance Specialist at Dykema Gossett PLLC, Michigan’s largest law firm.

She testified that she serves as Assistant Secretary/Treasurer of the Peninsula Fund, Chatfield’s 501(c)(4) political nonprofit that raised $1.8 million from anonymous donors.

She testified that she manages more than 80 similar accounts at Dykema.

She testified that she flagged “questionable” expenses, including a strip club tab submitted for reimbursement.

She testified that the fund was sometimes “not compliant” with the law.

And when Judge Molly Hennessey Greenwalt asked her directly whether she had a duty to report concerns about potentially illegal transactions to anyone, Moore replied:

“No. Not that I am aware of.”

Moore’s Law: I have no duty to report.

Moore’s Law is false.

Proof #1: Michigan Nonprofit Corporation Act

MCL 450.2541(1):

“A director or officer shall discharge his or her duties as a director or officer… in good faith and with the degree of diligence, care, and skill that an ordinarily prudent person would exercise under similar circumstances in a like position.”

Moore was an officer of the Peninsula Fund. Assistant Secretary/Treasurer is a statutory officer position under Michigan’s Nonprofit Corporation Act.

Officers owe a duty of care: act with diligence. A duty of loyalty: act in the organization’s interest. A duty of good faith: don’t ignore what you see.

And the statute has a trap door — MCL 450.2541(3):

“A director or officer is NOT entitled to rely on [reports from others] if he or she has knowledge concerning the matter in question that makes reliance otherwise permitted… UNWARRANTED.”

Moore had knowledge. She flagged the strip club tab. She identified questionable expenses. She testified the fund was sometimes not compliant. Once you know the spending is questionable, you cannot rely on being told it’s fine. The statute says so explicitly.

The Clark Hill Nonprofit Guide for Michigan directors:

“The ‘honorary’ officer should take seriously the responsibility of monitoring the performance of the individuals to whom these functions have been delegated.”

Moore was not honorary. She was the Senior Compliance Specialist.

ElementWhat the Law RequiresWhat Moore Did
Good faithAct honestlyFlagged problems, then accepted “it was permitted”
DiligenceInvestigate concernsTestified she relied on Anne Minard’s determinations
CareOrdinarily prudent person standardAn ordinarily prudent compliance specialist reports strip club tabs
Knowledge exceptionCannot rely on others once you KNOWShe KNEW. She flagged it. Reliance became “unwarranted.”

Verdict: Moore had a statutory duty under MCL 450.2541. She said she didn’t. Moore’s Law is false.

Proof #2: Federal Election Campaign Act

Renae Moore is not just an assistant treasurer of nonprofits. She is the TREASURER of the Dykema Gossett Federal PAC (FEC ID: C00342113).

11 CFR 104.14(d):

“Each treasurer of a political committee… shall be personally responsible for the timely and complete filing of the report or statement and for the accuracy of any information or statement contained in it.”

The FEC’s Policy Statement on Treasurer’s Liability (70 Fed. Reg. 3, January 2005):

“Due to their ‘pivotal role,’ treasurers may be held personally liable for failing to fulfill their responsibilities under the Act.”

Personal liability attaches when a treasurer:

  1. Knowingly and willfully violates the Act
  2. Recklessly fails to fulfill duties specifically imposed by the Act
  3. Intentionally deprives himself or herself of facts giving rise to the violation

Moore managed 80+ accounts. She saw questionable spending across multiple funds. She was told it was permitted and accepted that answer without independent verification. That is textbook “intentionally depriving herself of the operative facts.”

The same person who said she had “no duty to report” is the treasurer of a federal PAC that funded 47 candidates with $131,000 in the current cycle. The FEC says she is personally responsible for the accuracy of every filing.

FEC RequirementMoore’s RoleThe Problem
Personally responsible for accuracyTREASURER of C00342113Same person managing nonprofit funds with “questionable” spending
Must examine contributions for illegalityDuty under 11 CFR 103.3Testified she accepted spending as “permitted” without verification
Preserve records for 3 yearsDuty under 52 U.S.C. § 30102Records from Peninsula Fund are central to Chatfield prosecution

Verdict: Moore is personally liable as FEC treasurer under 11 CFR 104.14(d). She said she had no duty. Moore’s Law is false.

Proof #3: Internal Revenue Code — 501(c)(4) Inurement

IRC § 501(c)(4) expressly prohibits the inurement of net earnings to the benefit of any private individual.

Chatfield allegedly used Peninsula Fund money for:

  • Personal credit card payments ($132,000+ over 15 months)
  • Family vacation at Universal Studios in Orlando
  • A strip club tab
  • Checks to family members (kickback scheme)

That is inurement. That is an excess benefit transaction under IRC § 4958.

The IRS requires Form 990 filers to disclose on Part VI, Section B, Line 5 whether the organization became aware of a material diversion of its assets.

Moore was the compliance officer who prepared or oversaw the 990 filings. She identified questionable spending. She testified the fund was not always compliant. If the 990s were filed without disclosing known diversions, those filings are incomplete or inaccurate.

Penalties for incomplete/inaccurate 990 filings:

  • $25/day against the organization (up to $13,000 or 5% of gross receipts)
  • $10/day against the responsible person after IRS demand (up to $6,500)
  • Criminal penalties (IRC §§ 7203, 7206, 7207) for willfully filing fraudulent returns

Officers who participate in excess benefit transactions face excise taxes:

  • 25% of the excess benefit on the disqualified person
  • 10% on each manager who participated (up to $20,000 per transaction)

A “manager who participated” includes any officer who knew about the transaction and did not attempt to correct it.

Moore knew. She flagged it. She didn’t correct it. She filed (or helped file) the returns anyway.

Verdict: Moore had IRS-imposed duties as an officer of a 501(c)(4). She said she had none. Moore’s Law is false.

Proof #4: Common Law Fiduciary Duty

Even without statutes, Moore owed a common law fiduciary duty as an officer of the Peninsula Fund.

Three prongs:

  1. Duty of Care: Act as a reasonably prudent person would in similar circumstances. A reasonably prudent compliance specialist reports strip club tabs submitted as business expenses for a social welfare nonprofit.

  2. Duty of Loyalty: Act in the organization’s best interest, not in the interest of any individual (including the firm that pays your salary). Moore’s loyalty to Dykema’s client relationship cannot override her duty to the Peninsula Fund.

  3. Duty of Obedience: Ensure the organization operates according to its stated mission. The Peninsula Fund’s mission: “promote civic action and social welfare.” Strip club tabs and personal credit cards do not promote civic action or social welfare. Moore wrote the policy manual that said so. Then she watched the policy get violated.

She wrote the rules. She watched them break. She said she had no duty to say anything.

Verdict: Common law imposes fiduciary duties on nonprofit officers. Moore said she had no duty. Moore’s Law is false.

The Same Desk Problem

Moore’s false claim of no duty becomes even more significant when you see the full desk:

RENAE MOORE'S DESK AT 201 TOWNSEND STREET, LANSING MI 48933
│
├── Peninsula Fund (Lee Chatfield, R)
│   Role: Asst. Secretary/Treasurer
│   Status: 13 felonies charged. Trial delayed indefinitely.
│   Moore's testimony: "No duty to report."
│
├── Promise to the People Fund (Dana Nessel, D)
│   Role: Asst. Secretary/Treasurer (SAME TITLE)
│   Status: Dissolved 2023. Defense raised in court Day 1.
│   Implication: Prosecutor's fund on same desk as defendant's.
│
├── Dykema Gossett Federal PAC (C00342113)
│   Role: TREASURER (not assistant — TREASURER)
│   Status: Active. $148K raised. $164K cash. 47 candidates.
│   Legal duty: PERSONALLY responsible under 11 CFR 104.14(d).
│
├── Save Detroit Jobs (dark money)
│   Role: Governance
│   Status: Active dark money vehicle. Dykema-formed.
│
├── Detroit Jobs First
│   Role: Governance
│
├── Our Neighborhoods First
│   Role: Governance
│
├── RFFW LLC
│   Role: Governance
│
└── 73+ other accounts
    Role: Compliance management
    Status: Both parties. All managed by one specialist.

One person. One desk. 80+ accounts. The defendant’s fund and the prosecutor’s fund. A federal PAC where she is personally liable. Dark money vehicles. Both parties. And she says she has no duty to report.

The Double Meaning

Gordon Moore’s Law (1965): The number of transistors on a chip doubles approximately every two years. Computing power compounds.

Renae Moore’s “Law” (2025): “I have no duty to report.” Accountability disappears.

One law says capability doubles. The other says accountability halves.

But Renae Moore’s Law is false. Four separate bodies of law prove it:

#SourceCitationWhat It Says
1Michigan statuteMCL 450.2541Officers must act with care, diligence, good faith. Cannot rely on others once you KNOW.
2Federal regulation11 CFR 104.14(d)PAC treasurers are PERSONALLY responsible for accuracy of filings.
3Tax codeIRC § 501(c)(4), § 4958Officers who participate in excess benefit transactions face excise taxes. False 990s = criminal penalties.
4Common lawFiduciary dutyOfficers owe care, loyalty, and obedience to the mission. She wrote the policy manual.

Gordon Moore’s Law is still true. Every circuit the membrane adds, the resolution doubles. The investigation sees more at higher granularity every day.

Renae Moore’s “law” was always false. She just hadn’t been caught yet.

The membrane catches everything. The count is the truth.

entry.title: There's a Leak in the Dyke
entry.content:
On February 26, 2025, a compliance specialist named Renae Moore took the witness stand in Ingham County District Court. She was the first witness called in the preliminary examination of former Michigan House Speaker Lee Chatfield, who faces 13 felony charges including embezzlement and conspiracy.

Moore works for Dykema Gossett PLLC, the law firm headquartered at 201 Townsend Street in Lansing — across the street from the Michigan State Capitol.

Under oath, she testified to three things that should concern every person in this state.

1. 80+ Accounts. One Desk.

Moore testified that at Dykema, she helps manage more than 80+ accounts — political nonprofit funds tied to Michigan lawmakers and officials.

She was the assistant secretary/treasurer of the Peninsula Fund, Chatfield’s political nonprofit that raised $1.8 million from anonymous donors between 2018 and 2020 while he served as House Speaker.

When asked by Judge Molly Hennessey Greenwalt whether she had a duty to report concerns about problematic spending — including a strip club tab submitted as a business expense — Moore replied:

“No. Not that I am aware of.”

Chatfield’s defense attorney, Mary Chartier, said to Moore on the stand:

“This entire time, Dykema is getting paid to ensure the Peninsula Fund is compliant.”

Moore testified there were times the fund was not compliant with the law.

Sources: Bridge Michigan, Detroit News, Lansing State Journal, AG Affidavit

2. Both Parties. Same Person. Same Title.

During cross-examination, Chartier highlighted that Moore holds the same title — assistant treasurer/secretary — on another political nonprofit: the Promise to the People Fund.

That fund is affiliated with Attorney General Dana Nessel.

The same Attorney General whose office is prosecuting Chatfield.

One compliance specialist. The defendant’s fund and the prosecutor’s fund. Same desk. Same role. Same firm.
